Similar to FT, the HEFA process has largely been de-risked from a technical viability standpoint such that the remaining barriers are predominantly economic and market-focused. Specifically, the key challenges faced by HEFA are (1) sourcing low-cost and low-carbon hydrogen for the various hydrotreating stages and (2) sourcing sufficient quantities of the HEFA feedstock itself. Indeed, one of the most serious barriers to the widespread future build-out and expansion of HEFA surrounds the availability of feedstocks. An analysis of current HEFA feedstock supply provided in Figure 11 shows that utilization of traditional HEFA feedstocks—approximately a 55%-to-45% split across the food industry and biofuels, respectively—already exceeds domestic production by nearly 4 million tons per year, with the difference coming from imports (Rosales Calderon et al. 2024b). Further, future projections for HEFA feedstock supply show only a 14% increase in production capacity and imports out until 2032, casting some doubt around the long- term outlook for HEFA-derived SAF and emphasizing the need for supplementary solutions. As discussed above, some public concern surrounds HEFA-derived SAF due to the “food versus fuel” debate in using pure vegetable oils (for example soy and canola) which creates the perception of fuel in competition with food supplies. One proposed solution is to seek out new sources of oily feedstocks that do not directly contribute this debate, such as algae and rotational cover crops (e.g., camelina- and pennycress-derived seed oils). However, these next-generation feedstocks have not yet been proved at scale and are suggested to need further technological advancements, investments, and policy support to contribute significantly to future feedstock supply (Rosales Calderon et al. 2024b). 14 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. DCO = Distillers Corn Oil; UCO = Used Cooking Oil. 2.1.1.3 Synthetic Isoparaffins The third ASTM pathway certification came in 2014, known as SIP. Developed by Amyris and Total Energies, SIP is a multistep biological approach to produce long-chain hydrocarbons of the sesquiterpene family (TotalEnergies 2014). Based on recent small pilot- and demonstration-scale operations on the order of ~140 barrels/day, SIP can be viewed as approximately a TRL 7 pathway (Fuels and Lubes 2013). The core elements of the SIP process can be broken out into three parts: (1) enzymatic hydrolysis, (2) fermentation, and (3) hydrogenation, as seen in Figure 12. In the first stage, carbohydrate-rich feedstocks are deconstructed via enzymatic hydrolysis to separate, isolate, and recover glucose. Commonly studied feedstocks include sugarcane, sugar beets, and corn. The glucose recovered from the hydrolysis step is then fed to a fermenter, where an engineered yeast strain Saccharomyces cerevisiae selectively converts the carbohydrate stream into a specific class of C H sesquiterpenes known as farnesene.
